It was first used in 1834, in Mercadante's opera Emma d'Antiochia, and in 1836 Meyerbeer gave it a solo in Les Huguenots. Berlioz, Wagner, Verdi and Puccini followed, and twentieth-century repertory extended it to solo work, jazz and film scores.

A beginner should get used to the Boehm fingerings and key positions first, then practise the half-hole key under the left index finger, the low keys under the right thumb, and the automatic vent mechanism of newer models. The sound is an aerophone tone, and the pitch changes as keys open and close; modern models reach lower notes with extension keys.

Its body is thick and straight with much the same bore at both ends, and the cylindrical bore gives the clarinet family its particular way of sounding: it overblows at the twelfth rather than the octave. The range is over three octaves, and improved modern instruments approach four, with a lowest note the same as the bassoon's. Played softly it is tender, played loudly it has force, and the volume changes with soft and loud playing.

The bass clarinet belongs to the clarinet family, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.211.2-71. Modern types are mostly straight-bodied, with a curved metal neck and an upturned bell, a thick straight body with a cylindrical bore, usually Boehm or German fingerings, and support from a shoulder strap or a floor peg. It is played much as the clarinet is and sounds lower than written; it is common in symphony orchestras, wind bands, military bands, jazz, film scores, and solo and chamber music, played by clarinettists or by players who specialise in it.
